results.title: Enhanced Efficacy Contributes to Tropical Cyclone Intensification in Warmer Climates via Stronger Storm-Scale Radiative Feedbacks
results.abstract_crossref:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tropical cyclones (TCs) are expected to intensify in a warming climate as sea surface temperatures (SSTs) rise. Potential intensity (PI), the thermodynamic upper limit on storm strength, has long been used to assess how environmental conditions constrain TC intensity. However, a storm’s realized strength also depends on the efficacy in approaching its PI. Using a high-resolution (25 km) global TC-permitting model, we show that uniform SST warming strengthens TCs through concurrent increases in PI and efficacy, leading to a substantial rise in the frequency of category-3–5 storms. The increased efficacy persists even when changes in wind shear and ventilation effects are accounted for, indicating that changes in TC ventilation are not a primary driver of this response. Instead, the enhanced efficacy is associated with stronger coupling between radiation and moist static energy at the storm scale. This combined increase in thermodynamic limits and storm-level efficacy underscores the importance of considering both PI and efficacy when projecting future TC risks, as focusing on PI alone may underestimate the degree of intensification under warming. Storm-level radiative feedbacks should therefore be incorporated into projections to improve the predictability of TC intensity responses to climate change and variability.</jats:p>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Significance Statement</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Tropical cyclones (including hurricanes and typhoons) are expected to get stronger as the oceans warm. A prediction for this expected increase in TC intensity was based on the theory of potential intensity (PI). PI can serve as a basis to estimate and interpret TC intensity change under given environmental conditions. But a storm’s actual strength also depends on how efficiently it can use this available energy, which is referred to as relative intensity
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      , or efficacy, the ratio of actual intensity to PI. Using a high-resolution climate model, we find that warming oceans not only raise the ceiling for storm strength (higher PI) but also make storms more efficient at reaching this limit (higher
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      ). Importantly, this increase in efficacy is not explained by changes in wind shear or ventilation. On the one hand, warmer oceans sustain favorable conditions for longer, extending the window for storm intensification. On the other hand, stronger coupling between radiation and moist static energy may further enhance TC intensity. Together, in this model, these effects lead to stronger and more frequent major hurricanes (categories 3–5). This means that climate projections based only on PI may underestimate the risks posed by tropical cyclones in a warming world.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

results.title: Physical Processes to Cause the Seasonal Change of the Sea Surface Temperature in the Equatorial Atlantic
results.abstract_crossref:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The physical mechanisms governing the seasonal cycle of sea surface temperature (SST) in the equatorial Atlantic are investigated, with particular emphasis on the rapid cooling period from April to July. Using mixed layer and subsurface heat budget analyses based on reanalysis data, we identify pronounced zonal contrasts in the dominant processes controlling SST variability. In the western region, surface heat fluxes, including the solar radiation flux (SRF) and latent heat flux (LHF), dominate the seasonal cycle of SST. In contrast, in the eastern region, the vertical diffusion at the base of the mixed layer contributes comparably to the LHF. The seasonal modulation of these processes is strongly influenced by the mixed layer depth (MLD) variations, which alter the mixed layer heat capacity and regulate the response of SST to surface forcing and subsurface heat exchange. In the eastern region, the enhanced vertical diffusion is linked to both MLD variation and changes in the vertical temperature gradient at the bottom of the mixed layer. Subsurface cooling begins earlier than surface cooling and is primarily associated with upwelling below the mixed layer. This subsurface cooling strengthens the vertical temperature gradient and provides an additional contribution to the enhanced vertical diffusion during the cooling period. These results demonstrate how the seasonally evolving mixed layer and subsurface jointly shape the asymmetric seasonal cycle of SST in the equatorial Atlantic.</jats:p>

results.title: Effect of Spring Tibetan Plateau Snow Cover on the Frequency of Intense Tropical Cyclones over the Western North Pacific
results.abstract_crossref:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tibetan Plateau snow cover (TPSC) is recognized as a critical driver in modulating the regional atmospheric circulation. However, the critical role of TPSC in the frequency of intense tropical cyclones (ITCs) over the western North Pacific (WNP) remains poorly understood. Based on the observed and reanalyzed datasets during 1979–2023, this study reveals a seasonally lagged negative relationship between spring (March–April) TPSC and the frequency of ITCs over the WNP during the following peak season of ITCs (July–November). The analyses suggest that the sustainable hydrological effect of March–April TPSC enhances the upper-level convection heating and, in turn, intensifies the South Asian high until July–November. Then, the Rossby wave trains are excited, inducing a baroclinic structure with an anomalous upper-tropospheric cyclone and a lower-tropospheric anticyclone over the WNP. The resultant changes in the ITC-related dynamic factors, including enhanced vertical wind shear and suppressed midtropospheric vertical motion, create an unfavorable environment for the genesis of ITCs. Meanwhile, the low-level absolute vorticity and midlevel meridional shear of the zonal wind associated with the anomalous large-scale circulation further inhibit the intensification of tropical cyclones (TCs). Here, a physics-based statistical prediction model for the frequency of ITCs over the WNP is developed by incorporating spring TPSC and other factors. The model shows a robust predictive skill, with a correlation of 0.68 between the predictions and observations during 1979–2023. All of this highlights spring TPSC as an important upstream modulator of the ITC activity over the WNP, providing the mechanistic framework and a seasonal forecasting model for the frequency of ITCs over the WNP.</jats:p>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Significance Statement</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Intense tropical cyclones (ITCs), generally defined as the tropical cyclones (TCs) with maximum sustained wind speeds greater than 83 kt (∼41.5 m s
                      <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                      ), though accounting for only about 35% of all TC occurrences, contribute to approximately 80% of the economic losses and fatalities associated with the TC-related disasters (such as storm surges and flooding). Consequently, the seasonal prediction of the frequency of ITCs is particularly crucial. This study finds a significant negative relationship on the interannual time scale between spring (March–April) Tibetan Plateau snow cover (TPSC) and the frequency of ITCs over the western North Pacific (WNP) during the following peak season of ITCs (July–November). The analyses show that the sustainable hydrological effect of spring TPSC can significantly modulate the upper-level atmospheric heat content until the peak season of ITCs (July–November) and further influence the background circulation over the WNP through atmospheric teleconnections, thereby suppressing the genesis of ITCs over the WNP, particularly over the southeastern part of the WNP (SE-WNP), the primary source region of ITCs. In particular, we develop a statistical forecasting model for the seasonal frequency of ITCs over the WNP by integrating spring TPSC and other factors. The present study offers a useful seasonal forecasting tool for the frequency of ITCs over the WNP during the peak season of ITCs (July–November). This is helpful for formulating the disaster prevention strategies against the ITC-induced natural hazards over the East Asian coastal regions.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

results.title: How Regional SST Shapes Saharan Near-Surface Temperature: Sensitivity and Dynamical Mechanisms
results.abstract_crossref:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Sahara Desert has undergone substantial near-surface warming during the boreal warm season (June–November) in recent decades. Previous studies have suggested that historical and future Saharan warming is largely controlled by sea surface temperature (SST) changes. Here, we assess the sensitivity of Saharan near-surface temperature during the boreal warm season to SST anomalies at individual ocean grid points using Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) SST-patch experiments. To test the robustness of the results, we further validate the GFDL SST-patch responses using the Community Earth System Model (CESM). Both models consistently show that Saharan near-surface temperature is particularly sensitive to SST anomalies over the Mediterranean Sea, Caribbean Sea, and north Indian Ocean. Warming in the Mediterranean Sea and Caribbean Sea enhances Saharan warming, whereas warming in the north Indian Ocean induces Saharan cooling. The mechanisms underlying these responses are further examined using transient simulations and a potential temperature budget analysis. Results show that anomalous horizontal heat advection dominates the Saharan near-surface temperature response to SST perturbations, regardless of forcing location. Specifically, warming in the Mediterranean Sea and Caribbean Sea induces anomalous warm air advection over the Sahara accompanied by large-scale Rossby wave responses, whereas warming in the north Indian Ocean produces anomalous cold air advection associated with a Gill-type response and an intensified Azores high. These results demonstrate a strong basin dependence of SST impacts on Saharan temperature and underscore the dominant role of atmospheric circulation–driven horizontal heat advection in mediating the Saharan temperature response.</jats:p>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Significance Statement</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the sensitivity of Saharan surface air temperature to sea surface temperature anomalies in different ocean basins. We identify the Mediterranean Sea, Caribbean Sea, and north Indian Ocean as key regions influencing Saharan near-surface temperature. Warming in the Mediterranean and Caribbean Seas tends to enhance Saharan warming, whereas warming in the north Indian Ocean tends to dampen it. We further show that anomalous atmospheric circulation and associated horizontal heat advection in response to sea surface temperature anomalies are key mechanisms driving Saharan temperature changes. These results provide new insight into the drivers of historical Saharan temperature change and may help improve predictions of future Saharan warming.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

results.title: Wintertime Marine Cold Air Outbreaks over the Northwest Pacific: Lagrangian Climatology and Downstream Impacts
results.abstract_crossref:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Marine cold air outbreaks (CAOs), cold continental air masses outflow over extratropical oceans, are key drivers of wintertime air–sea interactions. This study presents a Lagrangian climatology of marine CAOs over the northwestern Pacific and marginal seas during the past 39 Januaries (1982–2020), focusing on their pathways, thermodynamic evolution, and downstream hydrological impacts. By tracking cold air masses that undergo ocean-induced modifications, we identify distinct regions of initial air–sea interaction and their associated transformation characteristics. On average, 46.1% of CAO trajectories first interact with the Sea of Japan, followed by the Sea of Okhotsk (18.5%) and the Yellow Sea/East China Sea (YS/ECS; 12.0%). They play a significant role in climatological surface turbulent heat fluxes, accounting for more than 80% of the total flux over the midlatitude basins. The most pronounced airmass transformation occurs within 2–3 days of the first interaction with the ocean with rapid heat and moisture uptake, as the air masses traverse increasingly warmer ocean surfaces. The characteristics of airmass transformations and downstream impacts vary by regions: CAOs over the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk, and Bering Sea tend to exhibit rapid moisture turnover. In contrast, CAOs over the YS/ECS more frequently exhibit prolonged moisture retention during subsequent air–sea interactions, contributing to a remote water cycle. Our findings thus underscore the importance of treating northwestern Pacific CAOs as a collection of distinct regional processes, each shaped by basin-specific air–sea interactions.</jats:p>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Significance Statement</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Arrival of cold air outbreaks over extratropical oceans is a major driver of wintertime air–sea interactions. This study tracks the movement and evolution of properties of these cold air masses interacting with the northwestern Pacific Ocean during the past 39 Januaries. We found that the arrival of the cold air masses over the ocean basins determines over 80% of the mean heat fluxes between the air and the ocean, and nearly half of these events occur over the Sea of Japan, followed by the Sea of Okhotsk, Yellow Sea/East China Sea, and Bering Sea. The most pronounced changes in temperature and moisture occur within the first few days of these interactions. Each ocean basin influences the cold air differently, affecting the hydrological cycle in downstream regions like Japan, Siberia, Korea, and Taiwan in unique ways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

results.title: Isolated Northern Hemisphere Cooling in an Idealized Model Promotes Ocean Carbon Storage and Glacial-like Ocean Features
results.abstract_crossref:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Earth’s past glacial cycles are paced by orbital insolation changes, but internal climate feedbacks modulating atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) are necessary to explain the full magnitude of glacial–interglacial climate variability. Identifying such feedbacks and linking them to orbitally paced forcing remains a challenge, impeding a comprehensive understanding of the glacial cycles. Orbital variations, determining the latitudinal distribution and seasonality of insolation, are primarily important for allowing the buildup of large Northern Hemisphere ice sheets. Meanwhile, the processes canonically understood to drive CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    drawdown and mediate ocean–atmosphere carbon partitioning are largely hosted in the far-flung Southern Ocean. This study explores the role of remote Northern Hemisphere temperature forcing in influencing Southern Ocean conditions that impact global ocean circulation and carbon content. In a set of idealized ocean–sea ice model simulations, we find that cooling air temperatures to glacial-like levels at the high northern latitudes (emulating the thermal effect of a large Northern Hemisphere ice sheet) drives a substantial CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    drawdown of 32 ppm—or 74% the magnitude of a simulation forced by globally glacial-like temperatures everywhere (43 ppm). Northern cooling is found to cool not only northern-sourced middepth waters but ultimately also global deep waters, resulting in a strong solubility-driven CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    drawdown component. It also drives several characteristic features of glacial periods, including expanded southern sea ice and a colder, saltier, and better stratified deep ocean, which contributes to air–sea CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    disequilibrium. These results demonstrate an interhemispheric connection between Northern Hemisphere conditions paced by orbital variations and Southern Hemisphere processes that modulate deep-ocean carbon content.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Significance Statement</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Linking the orbital pacing of the ice ages—primarily expressed by the growth and decay of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets—to processes hosted in the Southern Ocean that can regulate ocean carbon storage has long posed a challenge. Here, we demonstrate using idealized simulations a clear influence of Northern Hemisphere cooling on Southern Ocean conditions and global ocean circulation and carbon content, which in turn draws down carbon dioxide (CO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      ) from the atmosphere. This result underscores the importance of conditions in the high northern latitudes in shaping the ocean–atmosphere carbon balance, offering lessons about the interconnectedness of remote regions that are relevant to both past and contemporary climate change.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
results.abstract_openalex: Abstract Earth’s past glacial cycles are paced by orbital insolation changes, but internal climate feedbacks modulating atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) are necessary to explain the full magnitude of glacial–interglacial climate variability. Identifying such feedbacks and linking them to orbitally paced forcing remains a challenge, impeding a comprehensive understanding of the glacial cycles. Orbital variations, determining the latitudinal distribution and seasonality of insolation, are primarily important for allowing the buildup of large Northern Hemisphere ice sheets. Meanwhile, the processes canonically understood to drive CO 2 drawdown and mediate ocean–atmosphere carbon partitioning are largely hosted in the far-flung Southern Ocean. This study explores the role of remote Northern Hemisphere temperature forcing in influencing Southern Ocean conditions that impact global ocean circulation and carbon content. In a set of idealized ocean–sea ice model simulations, we find that cooling air temperatures to glacial-like levels at the high northern latitudes (emulating the thermal effect of a large Northern Hemisphere ice sheet) drives a substantial CO 2 drawdown of 32 ppm—or 74% the magnitude of a simulation forced by globally glacial-like temperatures everywhere (43 ppm). Northern cooling is found to cool not only northern-sourced middepth waters but ultimately also global deep waters, resulting in a strong solubility-driven CO 2 drawdown component. It also drives several characteristic features of glacial periods, including expanded southern sea ice and a colder, saltier, and better stratified deep ocean, which contributes to air–sea CO 2 disequilibrium. These results demonstrate an interhemispheric connection between Northern Hemisphere conditions paced by orbital variations and Southern Hemisphere processes that modulate deep-ocean carbon content. Significance Statement Linking the orbital pacing of the ice ages—primarily expressed by the growth and decay of Northern Hemisphere ice sheets—to processes hosted in the Southern Ocean that can regulate ocean carbon storage has long posed a challenge. Here, we demonstrate using idealized simulations a clear influence of Northern Hemisphere cooling on Southern Ocean conditions and global ocean circulation and carbon content, which in turn draws down carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) from the atmosphere. This result underscores the importance of conditions in the high northern latitudes in shaping the ocean–atmosphere carbon balance, offering lessons about the interconnectedness of remote regions that are relevant to both past and contemporary climate change.
